title: Carney calls Trump's fresh tariffs a 'miscalculation' after trade talks collapse
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a fresh wave of US tariffs on Canada is a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us", after trade talks col
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a fresh wave of US tariffs on Canada is a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us", after trade talks collapsed late on Friday."They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday, adding that that the US and Canada were now in a trade "war". "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said. The prime minister confirmed he would match US tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics.The collapse of the trade talks upends a deeply integrated trading relationship, with no clear path to resolution. US President Donald Trump has yet to comment."We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.Now that talks have broken down, Canada has been hit with new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.The new tariffs are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said. Leaders of other federal parties in Canada, including the Conservative opposition, voiced support for the prime minister, as have the leaders of some Canadian provinces.Tariffs - a tax placed on imports from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home.Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers and have disrupted and damaged the global economy.Carney's speech on Saturday was his first address to Canadians after he announced late on Friday night that a deal would not be reached, accusing the Americans of making "last-minute changes" that were "unfair" and "uneconomic". US negotiators, meanwhile, accused Canada of making "new demands and walk backs" on terms which had been previously agreed.On Saturday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News there were no plans to resume talks.He added that the US had been prepared to cut some of its tariffs on Canada as part of the ill-fated deal.Carney, however, said the US presented "unacceptable" terms that were too restrictive, including curbing Canada's ability to strike new trade deals with other countries.He also rejected the assertion that Canada had made last-minute requests: "We clarified what was on offer and were continually disappointed by the answers."Doug Ford, the leader of Canada's most populous province Ontario, backed Carney and said Trump "can't be trusted". British Columbia Premier David Eby said the US demand for restrictions on Canada's ability to have other trade deals "would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state"."It was never acceptable to Canadians," Eby said. The Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also appeared to support Carney, calling the latest US levies "unjustified".Quebec's premier, Christine Fréchette, warned jobs would likely be lost as a result of the new US tariffs."Behind these numbers are real people," she said, vowing to introduce measures to support impacted sectors.Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose oil-rich province has worked to make inroads with the Trump administration, urged both sides to resume talks.The collapse comes after more than a year of on-again, off-again trade talks, which intensified in recent weeks after a US-imposed deadline to strike a deal or face further tariffs.The two countries were also engaged in a mandatory review of an existing North American free trade agreement, known as USMCA, with Mexico. The pact was signed by Trump during his first term to replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. It underpins $1.6tn (£1.2tn) in annual trilateral trade across Canada, the US and Mexico. Earlier this summer, Canada and Mexico had formally requested for USMCA to be renewed for another 16 years. The US, however, declined to renew it in its current form.Asked how Friday's trade talk collapse would impact the North American free trade pact, Carney said it was "certainly not good news".

schema.headline: Carney calls Trump's fresh tariffs a 'miscalculation' after trade talks collapse

title: Fear and fallout three months on from Northern Ireland's race riots
description: The rioting began after footage of a brutal knife attack was widely circulated on social media. The clip was shared by far-right activist Tommy Robins
body: The rioting began after footage of a brutal knife attack was widely circulated on social media. The clip was shared by far-right activist Tommy Robinson, as well as by Elon Musk, racking up millions of views on his X platform.A call for peaceful anti-immigration protests that evening gave way to violent scenes, mostly in loyalist areas.Protesters were told to target the homes of refugees and asylum seekers, but any person of colour was at risk, with rioters shouting "foreigners out" as they broke down doors and windows in homes across Belfast.Revisiting those dark nights almost three months later, it's clear the reverberations are still being felt among communities, particularly as officials continue to count the cost of supporting those displaced.As the chaos spread, many were forced out of their homes with nothing more than the clothes they were wearing.Northern Ireland's social housing authority, the Housing Executive, has said 76 households presented to it as homeless following 48 hours of violence, while community workers on the ground said that number was much higher, when including those who went to stay with friends or left the country.But, at the same time as social media posts were circulating organising the riots, something else was happening online.A network of groups normally helping migrant communities with things like food banks and interpreter support got together on WhatsApp.They helped more than 200 people, often rushing into areas of violence to take those targeted to safety.Anne works for one of the groups and described messages as "coming in as fast as people could pick them up"."And even then, when we were down town collecting people, we were then also being asked to go somewhere else, you know, to pick somebody else up."There's a lift needed to take somebody to work, lift needed to take somebody into the hospital for a shift. There's somebody coeliac, no food in the house, pick up such and such at an address."Ciara, another community worker, responded to a call from four Sudanese women fearing that their home would be targeted."I was trying to reassure them. I don't speak Arabic and they were just coming along. It was blind trust. But then I was on adrenaline thinking: 'I have to keep these people safe'."Imagine you were being brought somewhere and you didn't know where you were going. I just thought:  'God, these poor people might not even understand what I'm saying'."Then there was Carolyn, a community worker of 35 years experience. Her effort was gargantuan.She has a large home 60 miles away from Belfast and, with the help of a coach driver and his vehicle, managed to take 22 people out of the city to her house in County Antrim, where they stayed for a week."It was dark, nearly midnight, when they got here, and there was a lot of crying and hysteria from the kids and the families, just not knowing where they were and stuff like that. They were traumatised."Some of them, she recalled, didn't have a change of clothes. A mum with a baby didn't have nappies or formula."It was crazy. To think of how you would just flee your home, not able to take anything with you and try and protect you and your kids."East Belfast, parts of which are loyalist, was one of the hotspots of violence.Brian Anderson, a Methodist minister with the East Belfast Mission, said the narrative that loyalist communities are losing out to those in republican areas is deeply ingrained."It's perceived within loyalist communities that the other side are getting. And we are losing," he said."We're losing our culture. Houses are not being developed. We're losing our jobs. And, so, you put it into that context of them winning and the perception that we're losing. That's the green-orange issue.""You then bring other colours of nationality into it," he added. "They, then sadly, have become the target for a small minority of people."He said there had always been a "silent majority" against violence in Northern Ireland's recent history, but a "vocal minority who have been for violence, and they seem to hold sway"."We still have a problem in loyalist communities whereby if we have something we're cross about or angry about or don't understand or feel threatened by, we seem to turn to violence," he said.

schema.headline: Fear and fallout three months on from Northern Ireland's race riots

title: US military newspaper editor voices censorship fears after being fired
description: Even though partially funded by the Pentagon, Stars and Stripes has been editorially independent - through a congressional mandate and DoD rules.The n
body: Even though partially funded by the Pentagon, Stars and Stripes has been editorially independent - through a congressional mandate and DoD rules.The newspaper's Middle East reporter Lara Korte said she had also been told she was fired.Both Slavin and Korte say their dismissals - both for insubordination - relate to an interview they gave to CBS's Sunday Morning programme last month, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.Stars and Stripes reported that publisher Max Lederer was also fired.He had announced his retirement on Tuesday, saying his understanding of the paper's value and mission differed in "fundamental ways" from the Pentagon's plans for the publication.Slavin, who has worked for the paper for 21 years, told the PM programme that he had not been given an official explanation for his dismissal - and was considering his response even though he was not allowed to appeal. He said he did not know if it had to do with his paper's original reporting of conditions aboard USS Abraham Lincoln - the warship which has been deployed in the Gulf for months as the US-Israeli war with Iran continues. The vessel has spent a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days and family members of sailors aboard have expressed concern about their mental health, with some sailors having reportedly attempted to jump overboard.But Slavin said his dismissal came in a climate where the Pentagon had not had a press conference since May, and where journalists had refused attempts to interfere with their reporting. For her part, Korte wrote on X: "It's a shame for the institution and service members, who swore to defend the Constitution and deserve the right to a free and independent press."The president of the National Press Club, Mark Schoeff Jr, described Slavin's firing as "another brazen attempt by the Pentagon to dictate coverage of the military and should be immediately reversed".An average of 1.4 million people consume Stars and Stripes's content daily, mostly online, according to CBS. The paper is still printed outside the US for members of the military in places with unreliable internet access.In October, leading US news outlets rejected a new policy which barred journalists from entering the building unless they only reported information officially authorised by the DoD.  At the time, the New York Times, Washington Post, CNN and the BBC were among the major outlets which said they would not agree to the new rules. The Trump administration argued that the changes were needed to protect national security.In April 2025, a US judge ordered the administration to restore the Associated Press's access to presidential events after it was blocked in a dispute over the term "Gulf of America".   A few months prior, the White House broke with tradition and took control of the press pool which covers the US presidency.

schema.headline: US military newspaper editor voices censorship fears after being fired

title: Cardiff baby gets life-saving heart op - but needs a transplant
description: Baby whose parents feared had just days to live is 'thriving' after life-saving heart operationImage source, Family PhotoImage caption, Baby Macs was
body: Baby whose parents feared had just days to live is 'thriving' after life-saving heart operationImage source, Family PhotoImage caption, Baby Macs was facing death if he did not have a Berlin Heart fittedByNewyddion S4C chief correspondentA baby, whose parents feared had just days to live, is "thriving" after having life-saving operations on his heart.Macs Green, a previously "completely healthy baby" suffered two cardiac arrests and was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy - which can lead to heart failure.After a struggle to find suitable hospital beds, he has now had device called a Berlin Heart, external fitted, which takes over the function of his heart.But he still needs a transplant and doctors have told his parents Catrin and Dylan they do not know how long the wait will be before he gets one.But, after his operation in Newcastle's Freeman Hospital, Dylan said Macs was already "completely different" from how he was before.Before surgery he had been in a specialist unit in Bristol Royal Children's Hospital on an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, external (Ecmo) machine, which helped pump oxygenated blood around his body.Figure caption, Baby Macs 'thriving' after getting lifesaving treatmentTown planner Dylan, 35, told Newyddion S4C, external: "There was talk of end of life at that point. We're so pleased he's on the Berlin Heart."It means he can come off the drugs which have been sedating him. Since then, he's a completely different baby."He's smiling, he's responding to us. Before now, he's just been a small baby lying on a bed."Solicitor Catrin said, since the operation, it was like "having our baby back" for the couple, who have two other children, Caio, five, and Gruff, and that Macs had been "absolutely thriving"After multiple surgeries, Macs' Berlin Heart was fitted on 7 August after leaving  Bristol for Newcastle.A Berlin Heart is a type of ventricular assist device, external - an air-driven pump that sits outside the body and takes over the job of the heart by pumping blood around the body.The NHS Blood and Transplant team said 17 of these had been fitted in children across the UK in 2024-25.Image source, Family PhotoImage caption, Mcs's Berlin Heart has taken over the function of his own heart, but he still needs a transplantCatrin, 32, said the family, from Cardiff, were now waiting for a real heart for Macs."They've told us... he's likely to have to wait 18 months for a heart. It could be two years, it could be more than that."But a heart could also turn up tomorrow."If we knew we were just waiting and living in a hospital that would be fine, but there are a lot of potential risks that come with being on a Berlin Heart and a lot of things which can affect him."We just hope now he can remain stable."Image source, Family PhotoImage caption, Mum Catrin said it was like "having our baby back"The family are now urging parents to consider organ donation should they lose a child and thanked the hospital staff and others who have supported them."We are extremely grateful," said Dylan.

schema.headline: Cardiff baby gets life-saving heart op - but needs a transplant

title: Erin Patterson: The hotel booking snafu that could free mushroom murderer
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Erin Patterson is trying to overturn her convictionsByTiffanie TurnbullSydneyLast July, hundreds desc
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Erin Patterson is trying to overturn her convictionsByTiffanie TurnbullSydneyLast July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal."The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.Towns overwhelmed by frenzyImage caption, The fatal lunch was hosted at Erin Patterson's home in Leongatha in July 2023 When Patterson served her estranged husband's relatives a poisonous mushroom-laced lunch in 2023, killing three and gravely injuring another, she thrust the sleepy Gippsland region into the global spotlight.The community of Korumburra, where the victims were beloved figures, became shrouded in grief. Leongatha, where Patterson lived, was gripped by shock. And Morwell, host of the lengthy trial, was overwhelmed by journalists, lawyers and spectators - as were towns nearby.You couldn't walk down the main street without spotting some of the courtroom's stars, or grab a coffee without overhearing chatter about the case.It was this frenzy from which the jury of 12 needed protection, the trial judge decided.Jurors are required to consider only the evidence presented to them in court, and must only talk about the case among themselves. In Australia, these rules are so strict that discussion with outsiders is forbidden even after a trial wraps up.To reduce the risk of contamination and the temptation of gossip, Justice Christopher Beale decided the jury should be sequestered once deliberations began - a relatively rare move which meant they would stay in supervised accommodation with little to no contact with the outside world until they reached a decision.But finding the jury, and the jury keepers watching them, somewhere to sleep became something of a logistical nightmare.As the trial dragged on, stays became longer than anyone anticipated and accommodation became a constant scramble.And the week the table tennis tournament came to town - which by a stroke of bad luck was the one in which the jury finally retired - turned the accommodation drought into a famine.Early morning email revelationsAt 08:28 on Monday 7 July, an email from the judge's chambers popped into the inboxes of the lawyers in the case.It revealed that the lead detective who investigated the murders - a key trial witness - and two prosecution solicitors had been staying at the same hotel as the sequestered jury.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Detective Senior Constable Stephen Eppingstall led the murder investigationsThe jurors had exclusive use of a separate floor of the hotel, the email said, and had eaten their meals in a conference room, away from all other guests.Common areas like the lobby were used by everyone, but the jury keeper who reported the issue said there had been no interaction between his charges and anyone from the prosecution case."I understand that there is a shortage of accommodation in the district, but it is obviously undesirable," Justice Beale wrote.About two hours later, the prosecution responded, admitting they had been aware of the situation for days.The detective "took steps to avoid common areas from the point that he became aware that [the jurors] were there", their email read.Upon learning their team would cross over with the jury for a single night, the prosecution had done its best to find other hotels for staff. But they couldn't get alternative rooms for two solicitors, though the email stressed the pair also took steps to avoid any "incidental contact".However, another missive from the judge's chambers quickly overshadowed the hotel snafu that same afternoon: the jury had reached their verdicts.They had found Patterson guilty on all counts.Figure caption, Moment Erin Patterson is sentenced to life in prison'Most critical week of trial'Patterson's lawyers are now arguing the hotel mix-up amounted to a "fundamental irregularity" which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts."We would describe... it as catastrophic," Patterson's appeal counsel, Edney, told Victoria's Court of Appeal this week."What occurred here was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure in the process."The defence - which Edney pointed out had been kept in the dark several days longer than anyone else - didn't immediately move for a mistrial last July.Instead, it twice asked the state's juries commissioner to investigate in the weeks following the verdicts. Both requests were rejected, the barrister said, and the reasons have not been made public.A year on, there remains a "vacuum of evidence" around what occurred during "the most critical week" of the entire trial, Edney argued.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Patterson's legal team, lead by Richard Edney (centre)There is no CCTV from the hotel; no sworn statements from those who were sharing it with the jury - a group which also includes an unknown number of journalists; and nothing to say what happened except the two brief emails sent last July.There was also at least one media report at the time - raised by Edney this week but rubbished by the prosecution lawyers as "unverified" and "seemingly inaccurate" - that the mix-up had led to "people hiding in doorways to avoid contact" and "skipping breakfast"."My question is... so what?" Justice Peter Kidd bit back.In any criminal trial, jurors see other parties all the time - in corridors, or even nearby cafes - but they're under the constant supervision of jury keepers who have sworn to ensure there's no improper communication, he said.Edney conceded there was "no evidence" that the jurors had communicated with anyone else, but said innocent contact - even just seeing the detective or solicitors - could have resulted in "subconscious influence"."This was a hotel with windows," Edney said several times - a likely thing for it to have, someone from the judge's bench countered.Patterson's team cited two cases to support their argument: one in which jurors were discharged when one was offered a throat lozenge by a defendant's relative during a coughing fit, and another in which a retrial was ordered after jurors caught a taxi without being escorted by a jury keeper.Figure caption, Watch: 'Catastrophic' hotel mix-up at the heart of Australia's mushroom murderer appealThe prosecution's response was simple."The system worked as it was intended to work," Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane KC said.The jury was constantly supervised, and when a potential problem was identified, steps were immediately taken to prevent it becoming an actual issue.The jury keeper, the lead detective, and the prosecution all say there was no contact."The evidence in this case is that there was no interaction between any other person and the jury," he said.Other cases the defence pointed to in which jury errors resulted in retrials all had evidence of actual contact, he noted."That's not the situation here."Patterson has seven appeal grounds - the others relating to rulings on evidence and alleged unfairness by the prosecution - but this one, by the defence's own admission, is unprecedented.Just as important as actual interference is the perception of interference, said Edney, quoting the trial judge's own speech as he selected jury members on the very first day of the trial."Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done."The trio of judges are now deliberating on Patterson's appeal, as well as an argument by the prosecution that her parole period should be scrapped. They will announce their decisions at a later date.

schema.headline: Erin Patterson: The hotel booking snafu that could free mushroom murderer

title: Sheffield man speaks out on Devon mum who faked childhood illness
description: As a child, Matthew Johnson was known as "Britain's sickest boy" - but in reality, his illness was just a fantasy made up by his mother to gain public
body: As a child, Matthew Johnson was known as "Britain's sickest boy" - but in reality, his illness was just a fantasy made up by his mother to gain publicity and financial rewards.For six-and-a-half years, Lisa Hayden-Johnson claimed Matthew had a long list of illnesses including diabetes, food allergies, cerebral palsy and cystic fibrosis, but years later it emerged she had made it all up. Hayden-Johnson, from Torbay, Devon, was jailed and Matthew went into foster care and started a new life in Sheffield. Both were interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary called Love You To Death but after hearing his mother speak, Matthew said he had "mixed emotions" and it reinforced his decision not to speak to her.  Speaking to the BBC about how it felt to hear his mother's point of view, he said: "It was a lot of disappointment but I think also frustration as almost two decades on, there is still a lack of accountability from her side."When I could see, even after two decades... she still holds the same story and believes that she did the best by me... that obviously isn't right."Hayden-Johnson was 35 when she was jailed for three years and three months by a judge at Exeter Crown Court in 2010. The court heard her lies began when Matthew was born prematurely in 2001 and given a tube for feeding.He recovered but his mother insisted that this was not the case.

schema.headline: Sheffield man speaks out on Devon mum who faked childhood illness

title: ‘I can’t do the things my friends do’: Life as a teenage carer
description: Ava-Grace Britton is 17 and studying acting at college in north London. She likes going out, seeing her friends and wants to go to university next yea
body: Ava-Grace Britton is 17 and studying acting at college in north London. She likes going out, seeing her friends and wants to go to university next year.Unlike most of her peers, however, she also cares for her father, Paul, who has significant mobility and memory issues after suffering a series of strokes eight years ago.Along with her mother Karen, Ava-Grace monitors Paul's blood glucose levels, gives him medication and helps with dinner and jobs around the house. "I worry about him all the time," Ava-Grace told the BBC. "Before I go to college I help him and most days I have to return home quickly to look after him."She is not alone. Officially, census data suggests there are around 130,000 carers under the age of 18 in England and Wales.But the true figure is thought to be much higher, with many young carers hidden from view. The Carers Trust estimates there could be as many as 1 million carers under 18, with another 500,000 aged 18 to 25.For some the responsibilities are significant, amounting to more than 50 hours a week - with consequences on young carers' social and academic prospects. Paul's strokes were brought on by a sepsis infection, which he caught after cutting his thumb at work. His health is further compromised by diabetes which needs careful monitoring.His condition deteriorated so much he had to give up work as a borehole engineer. He is now cared for full-time by Ava-Grace and Karen, who runs her own charity which organises lunch clubs for the elderly and vulnerable."It turned our life upside down," said Karen."Paul spent three months in hospital and in rehab. I don't know how I would cope without Ava-Grace."Ava-Grace says her caring responsibilities have demanded a number of trade-offs over the years."You have to make sacrifices. I can't do all the things my friends do," she said. "At one point I was really enjoying dance and could have started competing, but it would have been a huge time commitment which wasn't possible.While enjoying college now, she had to move schools several times after being bullied and struggling with attendance because of her caring responsibilities and epilepsy, which she has to manage."I worry about the future," she said. "I really want to go to university, but can't imagine going anywhere too far from home. I know my dad needs me."Some support is available. Young carers are entitled to assessments from their local council to look at the impact on their health, education and wellbeing."When young carers get these it can make a real difference," said Andy McGowan, the lead on young carers at the Carers Trust. "But it takes many years of caring before they are actually identified. And then the support in place to help is patchy, it really depends on where you live."McGowan, who was a young carer himself to both his parents, says even when help is given to the young in the form of respite breaks, peer support and counselling, the underlying issue – the caring demands being placed on them – is often not addressed."The threshold to get adult social care from councils to relieve the caring burden is so high, many don't get help. Until that is addressed, the inequalities young carers face will not be tackled."The NHS could do more, he added, particularly in terms of preventative and early support for things like substance misuse and mental health, which are also contributory factors to the caring responsibilities young carers have."Often young carers are left to fight their own battles for too long - and so school and their own health come second," he said. In July, the government published an action plan for unpaid carers which included measures to support young carers, including improved help in schools and joined-up support between the NHS, social care and education. Other parts of the UK have their own policies – in Scotland, for example, there is a dedicated young carers' grant."Through our new national care service, this government is determined to build a system that recognises the extraordinary contribution of unpaid carers, supports them better and, in particular, helps young carers," a government spokesman told the BBC.For families like the Brittons, more help cannot come soon enough. "I worry about the impact caring has on Ava-Grace," said Karen. "She has had to grow up very quickly – that has had benefits, she is calmer and more mature than many girls her age and she has a real strength about her. But Ava-Grace and others like her need more help and understanding."

schema.headline: ‘I can’t do the things my friends do’: Life as a teenage carer

title: Energy UK says struggling households need more support with bills
description: Higher energy bills this winter mean the government should step in to provide more help for households most in need, the body representing energy firm
body: Higher energy bills this winter mean the government should step in to provide more help for households most in need, the body representing energy firms in the UK has said.Stubbornly high prices over the last few years have left some people needing "emergency support" over and above the existing £150 Warm Home Discount, Energy UK said.It added that bills were unaffordable for millions and a "better targeted and more agile" support scheme was needed.On Wednesday, the energy price cap for October onwards will be announced by regulator Ofgem and is expected to hit a three-year high."Suppliers continue to do all they can to help their customers but as well as persistently high bills, record levels of debt show how the current system is failing to provide the right support to those in need," Energy UK chief executive Dhara Vyas said.A new "social discount" scheme would result in "a system that works better for everyone", she added.Ofgem reported at the end of last winter that customers who had fallen behind on their energy bills owed suppliers a record £4.7bn. Since then wholesale energy prices have risen, following the start of the Iran war in February.Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight predicts Ofgem's cap on household price rises, which is set every three months, will go up by 4% when it is announced on Wednesday. The rise will apply to household bills during the first half of the coming winter and follows a sharper 13% rise in July.As well as the conflict in the Middle East, Cornwall Insight said prices had been affected by heatwaves across Europe that had increased demand for power generation to support air conditioning and other cooling.The price rise would outweigh the impact of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's move to remove VAT on household electricity bills from October, it added.Currently, people receiving means-tested benefits are entitled to the one-off £150 Warm Home Discount over the winter, something administered by the energy suppliers themselves. The rebate is paid for by a levy on all energy users that is collected and redistributed via bills.Energy UK said the Warm Home Discount reached six million customers, but there were another 2.5 million who needed help because a medical condition or draughty home meant they consumed more energy.It said if the government would allow the combining of information about customers' income, health and energy consumption, a discount scheme could offer targeted and adjustable support, and respond to changing needs and price levels.The body said its proposed new scheme would cost £1.9bn - nearly double the cost of the current scheme - but could offer £450 in support to some households.Energy UK suggested the new support scheme could continue to be part-funded through bills or shifted entirely onto the taxpayer, via government funding.The last time the price cap reached a similar level was in July 2023, Cornwall Insight said, which was still below the peaks reached the previous year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. During that energy price spike the Conservative government committed a total of around £40bn , externalof government spending to support households with energy bills. The challenge of combining sources of personal data, including income and health, and the proposal to find more taxpayer money to fund such a scheme are likely to raise questions.However, Adam Scorer, chief executive of National Energy Action, said this was the sort of approach his charity was calling for, especially as the Warm Home Discount has risen by only £10 over the last decade."We desperately need a new approach," he said."There will be a lot of detail to get right, but if government genuinely wants to provide breathing space for people in fuel poverty, it needs to take this challenge on and work with energy companies and charities to design something truly fit for purpose."

schema.headline: Energy UK says struggling households need more support with bills

title: Why do we love watching hoarder videos online so much?
description: Gordon, from Lincoln, believes videos on her account have racked up thousands of views because people are "naturally inquisitive" and "nosey"."We like
body: Gordon, from Lincoln, believes videos on her account have racked up thousands of views because people are "naturally inquisitive" and "nosey"."We like to have a little delve into other people's lives – in particular where there's a shocking 'before and after', or they're able to watch the process," she says."People find it really interesting and actually quite satisfying."Dr Wasim Ahmed, a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Hull, says it comes down to people craving a sense of control, curiosity and relatability."You're seeing something in the short-form video where it's creating tension, showing you a lot of mess, and there's a process and resolution that can be quite reassuring," Ahmed says."It's quite satisfying seeing a clear problem and a clear ending in just under a minute."Long before this sort of content became a social media phenomenon, programmes such as Britain's Biggest Hoarders, The Hoarder Next Door and Hoarder SOS were attracting audiences on television.Ahmed says the videos are going viral because social media platforms are "actively rewarding" this type of content.His current research focuses on social media virality, including why people are so captivated by short-form video."A lot of these algorithms learn from how long users are staying on these videos," he explains. "All it knows is that the person hasn't scrolled past."He adds: "So when there's a really filthy room and it's holding people's attention or it's a really shocking crime scene, the algorithm is reading that as a quality metric."It starts finding the user worse rooms, worse crime scenes, [and] allowing the content to be served up in greater numbers as well."Ahmed says another reason the videos perform so well is the level of engagement they generate through likes, comments and shares."People are quite drawn to the comments section, to have a scan [of] other people's views," he says."There is this concept of relation. There could also be a sense of comparison as well."Gordon says the main reason she posts online is to raise awareness, particularly about hoarding disorder and mental health.According to the NHS, hoarding disorder is a mental health condition, external in which someone collects a lot of things and finds it difficult to get rid of them, even when they negatively affect their daily life."I think it's really easy to be quite judgmental," she says."People see footage of these homes online and in documentaries, and it's really easy to judge and think the person's lazy."There's a lot of stigma behind it and a lot of misunderstanding."She says the stigma of being a hoarder can stop people from seeking help."This is real life. It's mental health. It's people who are finding themselves living in really unsafe, unsanitary conditions through no fault of their own."The more we can talk about it, the better. The less we judge, the more we can understand, [and that] is only going to be a good thing."Gordon says many of her followers are hoarders themselves."I get a lot of messages in my inbox saying, 'Thank you so much for your content. That house that you did last week, mine's not dissimilar to that and you're making me feel like I'm not the only one that lives like this'."A lot of people have messaged me and said that, because they've seen my videos, they found the courage to ask for help or maybe hire a cleaner."So it is having a really positive effect."Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds and Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

schema.headline: Why do we love watching hoarder videos online so much?

title: Kenya's gold rush: Was it sparked by the discovery of a $200 nugget by a goat herder?
description: Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river
body: Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries."Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential."I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend. He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says."We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged."We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs."I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services."This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold."We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty."If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

schema.headline: Kenya's gold rush: Was it sparked by the discovery of a $200 nugget by a goat herder?

title: A missing cat was found in Leeds after disappearing last year
description: Missing cat found 100 miles away in feral colonyImage source, Provided/Lucy RocheImage caption, Ginge was found almost 100 miles from homeByKit Taylor
body: Missing cat found 100 miles away in feral colonyImage source, Provided/Lucy RocheImage caption, Ginge was found almost 100 miles from homeByKit TaylorYorkshireA cat rescue charity in Leeds has been praised after finding a cat who had been missing for almost a year, 100 miles (160km) from home.Lucy Roche, volunteer branch leader for Cat Action Trust 1977, external, came across the ginger cat, called Ginge, while caring for a feral colony in Garforth, and noticed he was very tame.She took him to the vets and managed to use his microchip to track his owner in Sunderland and reunite them.Roche said the owner was in "flood of tears" when she called and could not believe he had been found.Volunteers from the charity visit feral colonies across Leeds, providing food, water and shelters to keep them warm.They also take cats in for veterinary care and neutering if needed.If the area is unsafe, they will rehome them, either with new owners or in rural areas like farms.Image source, Provided/Lucy RocheImage caption, Roche says she safely captured Ginge and took him to a vetGinge first appeared at the colony in Garforth a few weeks ago."I was stroking him and I thought he's so friendly he could be somebody's cat," said Roche.She was able to safely catch him in a humane trap and take him to the vets. There, they managed to find Ginge's microchip and locate his owner in Sunderland.Ginge came home with Roche while she waited for his owners to come and collect him."He was snuggled up next to me and was flat out snoozing because he was so tired."I don't think he's had a good night's sleep in ages."Image source, Provided/Lucy RocheImage caption, Ginge slept on Lucy's sofa while waiting for his ownersThe next day, Ginge was reunited with his owner, Beth.A video of the two reuniting was shared on social media, and Ginge is now famous around the world."We've had people from America, New Zealand saying what a wonderful story it is," Roche said."The support has been overwhelming."She also highlighted that reuniting Ginge with his owner was only because he had been microchipped.Image source, Provided/Lucy RocheImage caption, Ginge was reunited with his owners after almost a yearMicrochipping for cats became a mandatory requirement in 2024, external, and Roche said it is crucial for helping rescue charities to return lost cats to their owners.  The rescue branch in Leeds is run entirely by volunteers, and Roche said their work is more important than ever before, with "non-stop calls for help" every day."So many cats are getting abandoned, lost or injured."We just want to make life better for all cats."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: A missing cat was found in Leeds after disappearing last year

title: Dutch Grand Prix: Lando Norris says he is expecting a challenge for victory at Zandvoort
description: Lando Norris starts the first grand prix after Formula 1's summer break in the same place as he started the one before it - on pole.But the McLaren dr
body: Lando Norris starts the first grand prix after Formula 1's summer break in the same place as he started the one before it - on pole.But the McLaren driver does not expect the Dutch Grand Prix to end with the comfortable victory he enjoyed in Hungary a month ago.The lessons of the sprint race earlier on Saturday make Norris cautious heading into Sunday's race at Zandvoort.He started second to Mercedes' George Russell for the sprint, a reverse of their places on the grand prix grid. But Russell took a comfortable win while Norris fell behind Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in the closing stages.Norris is wary of something similar happening again."I'm not thinking of tomorrow," he said, "just thinking: I'm on pole. Let me enjoy it. I will do my preparation tonight, prepare well, learn as much as we can from this morning, see what we can do better."Norris took pole with a lap right on the ragged edge."We could have been on pole yesterday," he said. "The sprint race disappointed me quite a bit because of our pace."I knew we would be a little better come qualifying because of the low fuel and new tyres, and my final two laps I put things together a lot more."My final lap was not the cleanest or best lap I've ever done but I committed a lot more in my braking and took a lot more risks in the high-speed corners."It was a lap that was a lot more uncomfortable, one where I was hustling and sliding a lot more, reacting a lot more to the car - which is not necessarily the best way to go about qualifying but it worked today."Norris' lap exploited all McLaren's pace advantage through the corners in the middle sector. Here, including the daunting high-speed, downhill Turn Seven known as Scheivlak, Norris was fastest, 0.28secs quicker than Russell.That was enough to put him at the front of the grid, despite only being fourth and seventh-quickest respectively in the first and final sectors, which have more slow-speed corners.Norris' problem is that, in the race, an advantage in the high-speed corners cannot be exploited as much as on fresh tyres on one lap in qualifying.In races, F1 drivers often have to back off in the high-speed corners, to avoid putting too much heat in the rubber. This was the problem that led to Norris challenging Russell in the early laps of the sprint, only for his pace to drop off dramatically at about one-third distance."I'll see what compromises I can make between high and low speed," Norris said, "see how we can make our weaknesses not as much as a struggle."We just need to work hard. If we work hard and prepare well, it's possible. But I am not expecting a race like Budapest. I am expecting a challenge. But I am looking forward to it."Russell, who needs a good result to reignite his title challenge, is aware of this."They are very fast in the high-speed but I don't think that will give them as much of an opportunity to use that pace as in qualifying," he said, "because it puts too much temperature into the tyres. But pole is the best place to start, especially on a circuit where it's difficult to overtake."If Norris can keep the lead off the line to the end of the first lap, he has a chance. But still Mercedes' better pace, founded on a more-rounded car, could make them hard to beat in the race.For Russell, the minimum he needs on Sunday is stay ahead of Antonelli.Victory in the sprint, with Antonelli only fourth, moved him three points closer to the Italian, who dominated the first half of the season.But Antonelli is still 56 points ahead. That advantage is already imposing. The longer Russell is unable to reduce it as the races tick down to a season's conclusion shrouded in uncertainty because of the war in the Middle East, it will only become daunting.Russell has been on much better form this weekend, and has beaten Antonelli in all three competitive sessions so far. He says a mental reset over the summer break, which he spent with his fiancee, Carmen, and two friends, has helped him put a difficult first part of the season in perspective."The truth is, obviously Kimi's been doing an amazing job this season, and clearly the two of us have quite different driving styles," Russell said. "That was apparent last year, and it is really working well for him with this car and these tyres."And just trying to implement something similar into my driving style. I kind of describe it as, like, if you change your golf swing, you'll probably take half a step back before making those improvements."The break just allowed me to put those learnings into the back of my mind, come here this weekend, not fixating on what I want to try and achieve with the car and the tyres, but knowing in the back of my head what I need to achieve and just drive more freely."I'm really, really proud of that because it's just sort of building that toolbox of experience for me that's going to allow me to be even better in the years to come."After the break, I just feel way more relaxed. I don't feel like I've got anything to lose."The pressure's off. I'm just going to go out, enjoy it, and I don't even really feel in a fight. It's not mine to lose, it's mine to gain. So that's the mentality I've got, and I feel it's going to help me. I'm just enjoying driving."Russell, though, has Antonelli right behind him, and more than once this year the Briton has out-qualified his team-mate only to find him faster come the race. Not only that, but Antonelli also under-performed in qualifying.He was only 0.031secs slower than Russell, and 0.133secs off pole, despite a poor first sector to his final lap, where he took it too easy into Turn One, concerned that the drops of rain he could see on his visor would have affected grip levels more than they did."0.1secs off pole hurts a little bit because I had a really bad sector one in my last lap," Antonelli said. "It's never a good feeling when you see you are 0.2secs down in sector one."I was able to make it up in sector two and three but still not good enough performance-wise because I think we had a real shot today at pole."It was a very good wake-up call this weekend, that you can never lower your guard because when you do that... I did a mistake yesterday and today I did a mistake in Q3."So, it's not that I'm driving more tense or anything, but I just feel this weekend is a good wake-up call, and to just again put things in the right place at the right time and just deliver the result when it counts."

title: Hull City 2-0 Man Utd: Boss Michael Carrick says side won't change course despite shock defeat
description: Manchester United's fans had endured a bad enough day on the banks of the River Humber when Hull City's stadium announcer gleefully piped up midway th
body: Manchester United's fans had endured a bad enough day on the banks of the River Humber when Hull City's stadium announcer gleefully piped up midway through the second half.He had "an important announcement" for them. Two trains back to Manchester from the city centre station had been cancelled. The roar from the home fans matched that for their side's two first-half goals that sealed a first ever top-flight win over United - and first in league meetings since a Second Division encounter in 1974."You should have come in a taxi," they sang. Football supporters can be a cruel breed.As they were kicking their heels waiting for a train to take them back over the Pennines, the portion of the 2,400-strong visiting contingent that had chosen that mode of transport would have struggled to find any redeeming features."They didn't create much, which was the biggest worry," legendary former United striker Wayne Rooney told BBC Sport."When you play a promoted team, it's always difficult. First game of the season away from home, United just didn't seem ready for it."Former Newcastle striker Alan Shearer felt it was a fitness issue."I haven't seen Manchester United in pre-season. I saw them in this game and they didn't look fit, they didn't look ready to play 90 minutes of intense, high pressure, high-energy football," he added on BBC Radio Five Live.Well, I have seen Manchester United in pre-season; all six games of it.I wouldn't say it was a fitness issue. Until last weekend's defeat by AC Milan in Poland, no-one was questioning the fitness of Carrick's squad and six of his starting line-up returned to training on 9 July.It is an opinion though - and everyone is entitled to them; just as they are entitled to say Carrick's side were toothless in attack, before and after Marcus Rashford's half-time introduction for his first United appearance since December 2024.They are also entitled to say United don't seem to be able to defend solidly against opponents who play with wing-backs, as AC Milan did last week and Hull on Saturday.Skipper Bruno Fernandes felt it was a pressing issue as he told TNT: "Same mistakes as we did last season in every away game."We give too much of the ball to them. In the first 20 minutes the goalkeeper had more touches on the ball, too much time."We need to press a little bit more, be more aggressive, and set-plays - we need to work on it, to be more aggressive and try not to concede these types of goals."Set-pieces were a particular area Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic said he had identified to attack in the build-up to the game.The merits or otherwise of these opinions will now be dissected and analysed - and Carrick knows it.Portraying a calm presence in the teeth of such enormous publicity is one of his key attributes. It was in evidence again as he offered his view on the defeat."It's just one game, we're disappointed we haven't won," he added. "It's not more than that, it's not less than that."We've got to soak it up and come back stronger."It's the 'public' Carrick, the level-headed personality which is so different to the volatility of former United boss Ruben Amorim, who brought headlines, but also extreme emotions to the Old Trafford dug-out.However, the public face Carrick presents should not be taken to mean the defeat at Hull - who were beating their illustrious opponents in the Premier League for the first time, and inflicting Manchester United's first ever opening-game defeat to a newly promoted side - does not sting. It really does."I'm talking to you quite calm," he explained in his post-match press conference. "But I'm not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day, you know?"It's 100% not that, trust me, it's not that. Inside we're hurting but it doesn't mean we all have to shout and scream and come out and create some chaos. The calmness doesn't mean there's no emotion in it, for sure."Manchester United entertain another newly promoted opponent, Ipswich, next at Old Trafford on 30 August.Carrick said on Thursday it was "ridiculous" to think his side had been given a "favourable" start.What happened at Hull proved it.At least the £70m transfer of Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba has already been agreed, so it can't be claimed it is a 2022-style reaction to a bad start to the campaign."I know a lot goes on outside our football club," added Carrick. "I understand and I understand the responsibility I've got."I get it. We've lost today and there's questions to be asked. But it doesn't mean everything's wrong. It doesn't make me do things differently."
